title: Florida business owners allegedly scattered 1,500 mothballs on beach to send endangered birds packing
description: Two St. Pete Beach business owners allegedly spread 1,500 toxic mothballs on sand to stop black skimmers from nesting and are facing felony charges.
fullText:
Two Florida business owners have been charged with third-degree felonies after allegedly spreading about 1,500 "toxic" mothballs across a beach in hopes of keeping an "imperiled" bird species from nesting there.

If convicted, they could each face up to five years in prison, fines of up to $5,000 and up to five years of probation.

The problem started in late April when beachgoers noticed mothballs on the white, sugary sand on St. Pete Beach in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and bird-loving volunteers from the Audubon Society mobilized. They plucked about 1,000 of the small, white orbs from the sand behind the Plaza Beach Hotel.

Then 500 more appeared overnight.

The smelly balls containing pesticides dotted an area where endangered shorebirds known as black skimmers were "attempting to establish a nesting colony," FWC officials said at a news conference. Their placement also meant other wildlife and children "could easily come in contact with them."

It quickly became clear that someone might be targeting the birds, they said.

So FWC investigators flew into action.

The discovery of the mothballs ruffled feathers in the community.

There was "a lot of public outcry," expressing concern for the birds, while investigators tried to locate the source of the mothballs, FWC officials said.

Law enforcement served search warrants, combed through "terabytes" of data and eventually seized cellphones to try to locate the individuals behind the caper.

That work led them to Christopher Monroe, owner and manager of Chris's Beachside Bar, and Robert Czyszczon, owner of the Plaza Beach Hotel, FWC officials said.

Out of fear of lost revenue, the two allegedly hatched a plan to use mothballs to deter birds from congregating on the beach behind their businesses, authorities said.

Hikers Face $25,000 Fine After Off-leash Dog Barked At Grizzly Bear On Banff National Park Trail

Through video surveillance and receipt records, investigators found that Czyszczon spent about $60 buying "a large quantity" of mothballs at a Walmart the day before they first appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

Upon examining his phone, investigators found "incriminating" text messages between him and fellow business owner Monroe discussing their objections to the native fowl.

Text conversations revealed plans for placement of the mothballs on the beach, officials said. That's what led investigators to Monroe as a suspect.

The men discussed how they "were going to do something" to prevent the birds from nesting on the beach, FWC officials said.

Black skimmers don't nest in trees. They kick beach sand to make depressions on the ground. Then they lay their eggs and raise their young near the surf.

"They're the worst birds," one of the men allegedly wrote in anticipation of nesting season.

"The bird people will put up fence around the area, and then the beach people will not be able to get to and from because they will fence around that space."

Cellphone tower data showed Monroe's phone was at the same location as Czyszczon's phone on both nights when the mothballs appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

The men feared that nests on the beach would lead to fewer customers and less money being spent there, authorities said.

"Why didn't you tell me we lose $25,000 to $50,000?" one allegedly wrote in a text.

Monroe and Czyszczon were charged with illegal dumping, a third-degree felony, according to Pinellas County court records. They also were charged with the "attempted take of a state-listed imperiled species by harassment," a misdemeanor, according to FWC officials.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

About 6,800 black skimmers live in Florida. FWC officials estimate that several hundred live on the beaches of Pinellas County.

The pesticide in mothballs can harm people and wildlife that come into contact with their vapors, according to an educational publication by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (IFAS).

"With any pesticide, the label is the law," Brett W. Bultemeier, director of the UF/IFAS Pesticide Information Office, wrote in a 2021 educational publication about mothballs. "The label language is not simply a set of directions. Rather, they are requirements that are legally enforceable."

The birds probably weren't hurt by the "harassment," FWC officials said.

But it did delay their nesting, they said. That pushes the date that their young can fledge from the nest further back in the season. And that could put them in danger.

A big storm at the end of hurricane season, which ends on Nov. 30, "can wipe out a colony if those young birds haven't fledged yet," an FWC official said.

An attorney for Czyszczon did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. Court records indicate that Monroe doesn't have an attorney. He couldn't be reached for comment.

title: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual after the failed World Cup private investment plan - but it may not be that easy.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino stepped off a plane in Cali and was greeted on the runway by the president of the Colombian Football Federation.

Ramon Jesurun, a close ally of Infantino's, saw it as a chance to show his support, with the two men smiling in a photo opportunity for the federation's Instagram account.

Infantino had not travelled to Colombia for any run-of-the-mill meeting on Friday. He would attend the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Infantino was accompanied by Alejandro Dominguez, the president of South America's football governing body Conmebol, who praised both his record and the "enormously successful" 2026 World Cup, saying "we stand with Gianni".

This is the life of a Fifa president.

It involves building ties with some of the most powerful people in the world, shown by Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Before the biggest scandal to hit his tenure - the aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise plan - Infantino was an incredibly powerful figure who appeared bulletproof.

Now, after an apology and stated desire to withstand the backlash of his plan to sell a stake in the men's World Cup to private equity firms, Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual.

Uefa's threat to boycott Fifa tournaments still stands. That will be tested with the Fifa Under-20 World Cup set to kick off in Poland in 29 days.

Perhaps emboldened by the support he has received from outside Europe in recent days, Infantino is not going to stand down easily.

But what exactly is the role of the Fifa president?

A cavalcade of blacked out Mercedes, flanked by police cars, rolled into the Fifa headquarters in Rabat, Morocco, earlier this week.

Infantino had summoned a select few members of the Fifa management board to discuss his plan to sell off 21% of the commercial and ticketing business to a private equity firm.

This is how the Swiss-Italian travels - in between flights on the Qatar Airways Executive jet which has been made available to him. The plane enabled him to take up to three flights a day, watching two games, throughout the 2026 World Cup.

That type of arrival does look presidential - only more like a president of a country than a sports body.

It enables him to travel the globe, visiting Fifa's official offices like Rabat, where he was based over the past week as the Fifa Forward Enterprise controversy developed.

In his role Infantino is expected to visit the 211 member nations, to see the grassroots projects Fifa has funded.

Part of his remit is to unify football, which cannot be achieved from within the Fifa headquarters in Zurich.

It requires international travel to attend confederation meetings, and the global tournaments Fifa organises. Infantino needs to build relationships with officials and politicians.

In April, before the Fifa Congress in Vancouver, local authorities rejected a request for a level-four motorcade, usually reserved for heads of state or the Pope.

New Zealand police said they had declined a similar request during the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Alongside the cavalcade of cars and the private charter flights comes a large salary, too, three times what he first earned when elected in 2016.

Infantino, who was paid about £1.3m 10 years ago, now takes home about £4m - a base salary of £2.2m plus a confirmed variable bonus payment of £1.8m.

His predecessor Sepp Blatter was paid a £2.6m package for his final year as Fifa president.

Infantino gets a 'per diem' too to cover expenses and living costs, worth £20,500 a year on top of his salary.

As the head of the most popular sport in the world, it should be expected that there is a wage to match.

Infantino would argue that by driving record revenues and funding for member associations, he has proven he is worth the salary.

Infantino's alliance with Trump seemed to have elevated his status even further.

Many in world football felt that this began to come at the expense of his responsibilities in football.

In May 2025, Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress in Paraguay.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

There was also the Fifa Peace Prize, awarded to Trump weeks before the US invaded Venezuela to depose president Nicolas Maduro and launched air attacks on Iran.

Despite criticism, the Fifa ethics committee did not respond to complaints about Infantino's political neutrality over the prize.

At the start of the year, Infantino made a surprise appearance at the inaugural meeting of Trump's Board of Peace, set up to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza.

The International Olympic Committee, of which Infantino is an invited member, said its rules on political neutrality had not been breached.

However, many felt he had positioned himself too close to the US president.

This was heightened when USA striker Folarin Balogun escaped a ban after being sent off at the World Cup.

It was an unprecedented move by Fifa's disciplinary committee, with Trump saying he had personally called Infantino asking for the red card to be reviewed.

Infantino insisted it was a decision taken by an independent body over which no-one could have an influence.

On the final weekend of the World Cup, Trump and Infantino appeared together at Trump Tower in New York. The US president said he had called the Fifa president who "made another great decision".

Then, perhaps the culmination of Infantino's close association with Trump, came Fifa Forward Enterprise.

The private investor was to be a company linked to the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

Independent questions of Infantino's methods and decisions are rare because he does not often speak to the media.

In the past four years he has given just two news conferences, both lasting an hour and held before the start of the World Cup.

Other than that, Infantino generally appears in Fifa-produced interviews issued through their official channels.

Before the 2026 World Cup, Infantino tried to head off at the pass any queries about high ticket prices and supporters' visas.

But, at the news conference before the World Cup, his reply of "just, you know, chill, relax" about Somali referee Omar Artan, who had been denied entry to the USA at Miami Airport, sparked concern.

The Fifa statement issued on Wednesday offered some contrition. But there was a rebuke, too.

It gave Infantino the chance to bite back, saying Fifa would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process".

The allure of the role is great, underscored by the fact there have been just four permanent Fifa presidents since Stanley Rous was elected in 1961.

Outside of Europe, the record revenues achieved by Infantino have funded the football operations of many countries. That has created loyalty, and it is a vote winner.

Yet for Uefa, and a few other national associations, the rap sheet is now too long.

Fifa cannot be run as an autocratic project any longer, claim his critics - many of them within European football.

Expanding the World Cup was in Infantino's election manifesto, and an increase to 64 teams for 2030 seems highly likely if he gets a fourth term.

There was also the expanded summer Club World Cup. The trophy is engraved with a personal tribute - "Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino".

The unique allocation of the next two men's World Cups helped ensure Saudi Arabia, another close ally of Infantino, would get the 2034 event.

The draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair. Trump was front and centre, as was Infantino.

Many supporters felt the price of tickets was too high, while some who were prepared to pay for them were denied visas.

Fifa opted to use a secondary market place with uncapped prices and a 30% share on each ticket sold.

Critics said profit had become more important than the supporter experience, with the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey subpoenaing Fifa to answer questions about its ticketing practices.

Even with all these controversies, Infantino was expected to be re-elected, such was his support around the world in many member associations.

Indeed, before the World Cup 111 had already declared for him - enough to guarantee re-election.

Now that picture is uncertain amid the fallout from Fifa's failed private investment plan.

Uefa sees this moment as its chance to force him to step down.

But, as his attendance at the Colombia president's inauguration shows, that may be incredibly difficult to achieve.

title: Miami Heat legend Udonis Haslem ‘proud to announce’ ownership stake in Premier League soccer club
description: Udonis Haslem is expanding his business portfolio with an investment in a newly promoted Premier League soccer club. The popularity of soccer has skyrocketed in the US following the conclusion of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
fullText:
Udonis Haslem is expanding his business portfolio with an investment in a newly promoted Premier League soccer club.

The popularity of soccer has skyrocketed in the US following the conclusion of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The sport has gained a plethora of new fans.

This apparently includes Miami Heat legend and former NBA star Udonis Haslem, who has decided to pour in some of his hard-earned money into a newly promoted English Premier League club.

fullText:
President Trump's attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust.

The British broadcaster received approval from a judge late last month to probe the president's financial documents after Trump claimed he experienced losses due to an episode of the company's "Panorama" series titled "Trump: A Second Chance?"

In the footage, the BBC strung together three separate portions of a speech from Trump to make it look as if he encouraged a violent attack on the Capitol.

"The BBC's improperly broad subpoena demands the Trust's confidential tax, ownership, and financial records for approximately 400 entities," Trump's attorney Alejandro Brito wrote in the legal filing.

"Once the Trust were to begin handing those records over to the BBC, that disclosure could not be undone, and the Trust's pending objections could not restore what the BBC will already have seen," Brito added.

If the emergency motion is not approved, the BBC would be granted insight on Trump's crypto and stock profit, as well as business transactions from at least 400 entities and companies tied to his personal assets managed by family.

Last month, Judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett granted the BBC's subpoena to review documents from the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust dating to Jan. 1, 2023.

Her approval requires that the trust start producing documents by Thursday.

"Against the Trust's irreversible injury, the BBC cannot point to any injury, only to brief delay, which does not constitute harm. Fact discovery remains open for months, and the BBC has never explained why it needed a non-party's complete financial records within ten days or how a short stay would impair its defense," Brito wrote.

The BBC has apologized for the documentary edit but has strongly rebuked Trump's push for a payout and attempted to dismiss the lawsuit against the company, arguing U.S. courts hold no legal jurisdiction over the foreign corporation.

The president has refused to back down and recently requested that District Judge Roy Altman allow him to alter the lawsuit in a manner that would shield his financial documents from being reviewed by the British broadcaster.

fullText:
A business case for phase one of the Hereford bypass has claimed congestion in parts of the city could fall by up to 25%.

It also said journey times between the city centre and Rotherwas could reduce by an average of six-and-a-half-minutes.

Herefordshire Council decided to publish the full document ahead of work starting on the route, which will link the A49 and A465 south of the city.

Councillor Philip Price, cabinet member for transport and infrastructure, said: "One of the reasons we have produced a detailed business case is to demonstrate that the scheme represents good value for money."

About £45m has been put aside for the bypass, which will create an alternative route for vehicles to travel around the city.

The business case - which has been published by an infrastructure consultancy called AECOM - runs to 30 pages.

It forecasted that average daily traffic would fall by between 15% and 25% along Walnut Tree Avenue and the A465, both of which suffer regular hold-ups.

It also suggested a smaller drop in traffic of 7% along Holme Lacy Road, and listed "improved reliability of bus services" as one of the benefits.

Drivers would also benefit from reduced travel times between the A465 and Herefordshire Enterprise Zone, where 3,500 people work, of about six-and-a-half minutes.

The document also cited "quieter residential streets" as a benefit, with fewer drivers seeking to cut their journey times by using the well-known rat runs.

Price added: "Publishing the full business case is an important milestone in progressing the Hereford bypass.

"[It] sets out the benefits the scheme will bring, including improving connectivity, supporting businesses, unlocking growth and creating better places for people across Herefordshire.

"Delivering a scheme of this importance will require the support and involvement of the whole community.

"It represents an important first step towards a more connected and resilient transport network for Herefordshire."

The bypass has been divisive - residents have voiced concern over the cash-strapped council earmarking another £5m towards it, on top of the £40m that had already been committed.

The council is also in a legal standoff with a woman who is refusing to sell her land for phase one to start, due to an ancient tree in her back garden.

But bosses said they were confident work would still be able to start in December, with the first phase set to be complete in 2028.

Phase two, which would include a second river crossing over the River Wye to the west of the city, is subject to further funding and planning permission.

title: Weighing the Business Case for Quality
description: On the economics of doing great work.
fullText:
Most of us want to do great work. Building things of exceptional quality – work that’s beautiful, lovable, fast – is one of life’s great joys.

However, the story goes, capitalism doesn’t value quality. Businesses don’t fund software that is lovable. Thus, you need to make a career choice: do you want to be a craftsperson, or do you want to make money?

I mean, yes, these two things are in some tension. You can easily make money maintaining EOL plumbing if you can motivate yourself to do it well, and you can easily make beautiful products if you can afford to give them away for peanuts.

But there absolutely exist businesses that are very large and successful in part because they invest in quality. Beauty, speed, and user experience can drive profits.

Patrick Collison spoke about this back in 2023:

My intuition is that more of Stripe’s success than one would think is downstream of the fact that people like beautiful things, and for rational reasons. Because what does a beautiful thing tell you?

Well, it tells you the person who made it really cared. And you can observe some superficial details, but probably they didn’t only care about those and did everything else in a very slapdash way. …

If someone really convinced me that the financial returns to craftsmanship and beauty – which I believe are greater – are not greater, I’d still do it. Life’s too short.

So you could try working at Stripe.

Even within Stripe, however, there are products and areas that don’t justify the level of care Patrick describes here. To get a real mandate for quality – to do great work, and earn a good income doing it – you need to ask yourself a question: is there a business case for quality here?

If you want the resources necessary to build something well, then choose to work on things worth doing well.

There are a lot of reasons a product could be worth doing exceptionally well. Here are some:

There are many others, but even just the above attributes describe some of the most craft-centric companies out there: Linear, Figma, Stripe, Wealthsimple, Apple, and so on. The economic details vary, but if a large company is spending the surprisingly large amount of resources it takes to build exceptional products, there’s a business reason to do so.

Meanwhile, many of the most slapdash products out there are the inverse of this dynamic: imagine an internal control panel that an enterprise contract obliges you to deliver. A project like that shouldn’t be laboured over – it should be built to a minimum reasonable standard, then shipped. Its primary success factor is to exist.

So if your goal is to work on things that are worth doing well, how do you figure that out a priori? You need to get a sense of the business. Who are the customers, what makes them buy, and what makes them stick around? If you want to build a company that can justify making great stuff, ensure that you’re in a market where quality can confer an advantage.

The analysis is a bit easier if you’re being recruited, since you can simply ask.

Back when I ran Steamclock, occasionally I’d be approached by a prospective client that wanted to make a delightful app (excellent, that’s what Steamclock is all about) but for a use case that seemed… peripheral. Maybe it was an occasional-use product, or perhaps it was an internal tool.

Sometimes it was plainly obvious that hiring an A-Team for the project was overkill, but other times, I’d explicitly ask:

Thinking about what success looks like, how much do UX and quality for this product contribute to the success of the business overall?

Sometimes they’d quickly realize it was a bad fit. But other times, they’d make a compelling economic case for craft and UX – starting us off on the right foot to execute on that vision.

At the end of the day, there are countless ways to make a career building great software. The important thing to remember is that it’s not enough to care deeply about craft. It’s a great start, but if your customers won’t actually reward quality, you’ll be running uphill.

Instead, work on products that have a business case for craft. You’ll have a durable mandate to do great work – and make money doing it.

Not all of the lessons in the Walker Deibel playbook fit between its covers. One of the first bolt-on acquisitions Lucas Philips tried to close was a tiny shop in rural Oregon — a guy who had spent decades fabricating custom interiors for Porsches. Philips flew to Portland, grabbed a brand-new convertible Mustang on a free upgrade from his shiny new Hertz President's Circle card, and spent three-and-a-half hours driving south through "the most beautiful" Oregon landscape toward the seller's property. The owner had originally quoted $40,000 for the operation. Two days later, after watching Philips pull up in a gleaming convertible and spend time on site, he decided the price should be more like $320,000.

"I regret that so much to this day," Philips said. "I should have just taken the Camry."

Lucas Philips grew up watching his father do something increasingly rare among his generation: own a small business outright and still make it home in time for school drop-offs and hockey practice. At 26, he decided to do the same — acquiring a niche manufacturer of custom automotive interiors in Newark, N.J. Now 29, Philips told Fortune that he's glad he did it, but "it's really not for the faint of heart."

Since acquiring Newark Auto, Philips has pushed annual revenue from "a little over a million" at purchase to more than $3 million this year, in roughly five years of operating time. He's done it with bolt-on acquisitions, long commutes, and a roster of hourly workers who have never seen the perks of startup life — Philips jokes about the proverbial ping-pong table in the office — but he's also learned that in the world of small business, the smallest details can derail a deal.

Like: don't rent a convertible when you're making a business trip to try to acquire a new subsidiary.

Philips traces his entrepreneurial drive to something older than Northwestern. His family immigrated to New York in the Ellis Island era a little over 100 years ago and, frankly, nobody wanted to hire them. He's from several generations of Jewish small business owners, so it was only natural for him to think this way, he said.

The list of businesses is somewhat endless. One grandfather sold paper goods — boxes, plastic wrap — to the Jewish bakeries of New York. His father sold sunglasses imported from China before anyone was importing anything from China, then hair accessories, then bought a high-end custom furniture business that now has a showroom in the B&B building on Madison Avenue and a factory in Christiansburg, Virginia.

fullText:
As OpenAI chases rival Anthropic in the enterprise and tries to sustain growth in the face of new competition from cheaper open-source alternatives, the artificial intelligence company is seeking to reassure staffers that the business remains healthy.

In an internal meeting with employees on Wednesday, finance chief Sarah Friar and board chair Bret Taylor touted OpenAI's revenue growth and addressed competition with Anthropic, CNBC has learned. Friar said OpenAI's annualized recurring revenue in July exceeded the entire second quarter.

"And Q2 was no slouch," Friar said, according to a partial transcript of the meeting that was reviewed by CNBC.

Friar and Taylor said momentum was driven by the release of the company's GPT-5.6 series of models, its new enterprise agent called ChatGPT Work, and growing adoption of its AI coding tool, Codex.

OpenAI is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation as it gears up for a potentially massive IPO. The company faces a constantly changing competitive landscape that includes Anthropic and Google as well as a slew of so-called open-weight models out of China that can be accessed at much lower costs. Earlier this month, China's Moonshot AI unveiled Kimi K3, which claims it closes the gap with leading U.S. offerings and surpasses OpenAI and Anthropic's most capable systems on some benchmarks.

OpenAI has been racing to bring in new users, particularly enterprises and developers, in order to generate the revenue needed to help support its infrastructure spending plans, which are being funded by outside capital.

In February, OpenAI told investors that it plans to target roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. It's currently in discussions with Nvidia about a backstop of up to $250 billion that would help fund its plans to lease a massive new AI data center in Ohio, as CNBC reported earlier this week.

The staggering figures and the rapid rise of Anthropic, which surpassed OpenAI by valuation earlier this year, have raised questions about the durability of OpenAI's business. Anthropic said in May that its revenue run rate revenue topped $47 billion, up from the roughly $10 billion that it generated for all of 2025, as its Claude Code tool has become a huge hit with developers.

The Information reported in March that OpenAI had recently topped $25 billion in annualized revenue, citing a person with knowledge of the matter.

Taylor told employees on Wednesday that Anthropic had a strong start to the year, and he acknowledged that OpenAI had to play catch-up in the coding market. But he said he's encouraged by Codex's growth.

"You're seeing people who went deep on Claude Code, ended up with a very high bill, and started looking for an alternative," Taylor said at the meeting.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic confidentially filed for IPOs with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June. Neither company has disclosed additional details about when they plan to debut.

fullText:
It is clear from Tottenham's summer transfer business that they have big ambitions in the Women's Super League next season.

Martin Ho's side have strengthened in the market, building a squad that, on paper, could cause a stir among the league's top clubs.

They finished fifth in the WSL last season - a significant improvement on the year before when they flirted with relegation.

Tottenham broke their club-record signing this summer to bring in France defender Alice Sombath from Lyon, having spent around £375,000 on Signe Gaupset in January.

They also signed forwards Shekiera Martinez and Kirsty Hanson, defender Caitlin Dijkstra, midfielder Victoria Pelova and goalkeeper Selma Panengstuen.

So how have they approached their transfer business and what are the club's ambitions this year?

It is Spurs' seventh season in the top flight and their growth has been vast - the number of staff has increased and training facilities have improved.

They have their own base at the club's training centre on Hotspur Way but plans for a new women and girls academy facility was blocked in court this week.

Just months after promotion in 2019, they hosted almost 40,000 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium for the north London derby defeat by Arsenal.

A year later, they signed USA superstar Alex Morgan on a short-term loan after she gave birth and in 2024 they reached the Women's FA Cup final.

A disappointing season under Robert Vilahamn in 2024-25 led to his sacking and Ho's subsequent arrival, and Spurs jumped back up the table in his debut campaign.

Since Ho joined the club in July 2025, Tottenham have had a 12-month plan for recruitment and had identified targets in the three windows that followed.

Talks with striker Cathinka Tandberg and defender Toko Koga, who both joined in 2025, were advanced before Ho's contract was finalised and they have become key players under him.

Ho took time to look at the squad in his first summer to see what was needed before implementing widespread evolution plans.

Since then, sources at Tottenham say they signed all of their key targets in January and have already done the same this summer despite the window remaining open until 3 September.

There was a deliberate attempt to get deals wrapped up early so Ho could work with the entire squad for a full pre-season programme.

Meanwhile, managing director Andy Rogers, who has been at Spurs for 24 years, has led their transfer business this summer, keen to leave the club in a strong position and ensure a smooth handover before he steps down.

What that forward-planning and successful business does for Tottenham will be clearer at the end of the season.

They have consolidated their position as a WSL club and have enough off-field resources to start building towards European football.

Ho has been consistent in his messaging, stressing Tottenham's ambition is to compete with the WSL's best and to build a squad capable of playing in Europe.

With only the top three teams in the WSL qualifying for the Women's Champions League and with Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City and Manchester United dominating those spots, it is a huge step for Tottenham to make.

They also have to compete with fellow big-spenders London City Lionesses and Brighton, who themselves have ambitions of breaking into the top three.

Their investment and growth has been a catalyst for Spurs, who know they cannot be left behind in a period when transfer fee records are constantly being broken.

It is also a period in the women's game's development when discussions involving financial regulations and salary caps are still in their infancy.

That means clubs have the ability to pour in more money should they wish and with little regulatory fightback - though that could change in the near future.

Tottenham's spending on the women's side this summer has coincided with an ambitious window for the men's team, who are looking to bounce back from a poor campaign that almost led to their relegation from the Premier League.

It is part of an overall change in strategy following the departure of chairman Daniel Levy in September 2025 and subsequent movement in the boardroom.

Vinai Venkatesham also joined as chief executive officer from Arsenal in April 2025 and was crucial in their women's team's success, something he hopes to emulate at Tottenham.

Another huge challenge for the club remains the growth of the fanbase. Spurs had an average attendance of just 1,734 in the WSL last season - a figure that factored in higher-attended crowds at sporadic matches at the main stadium.

fullText:
PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game Studios
Halo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time

This 25th-anniversary remake of Xbox’s most iconic shooter comes loaded with symbolism. It arrives at a time when Xbox’s whole gaming division (and indeed the games business as a whole) is in turmoil. It’s been made by Halo Studios, an outfit that has arguably never quite recaptured the magic conjured by Halo: Combat Evolved’s original developer Bungie, a studio now owned by rival Sony. It has been polished and prettified using Unreal Engine 5, making it look and feel more modern at the expense of visual uniqueness: Halo now looks similar to hundreds of other games made with those same tools, where Bungie’s 2001 original, made with a bespoke engine, still looks austerely distinctive. I never wanted to become this person, but: perhaps things were better in the old days?

I had my misgivings after opening level, in which the freshly defrosted supersoldier Master Chief fends off an alien attack on a disintegrating spaceship. Originally this was a masterclass in explosive action: you wake up, you look around (once a clever way to determine whether you needed to invert the controls), and you get right into it, firing gaming’s best pistol at chittering alien grunts who scatter from your bullets. Now it’s wrapped in needlessly expanded cutscenes and explanations. Where Halo Studios has made changes to Combat Evolved’s pacing, it really feels noticeable.

After that, however, I spent much less time thinking about what has been changed, and much more thinking about what hasn’t. Nobody really makes single-player shooters like Halo any more: tense, adaptable, challenging. In 2026, we have multiplayer shooters of every imaginable kind; there is little reason for computer-controlled enemies to be intelligent and unpredictable, because we mostly play against other humans, and they provide infinite variation. What we don’t have in abundance in 2026 is atmospheric single-player shooters like this, or Half-Life, or System Shock 2. Solo campaigns in shooters such as Call of Duty have been reduced to flashy “cinematic” shooting galleries. Halo: Campaign Evolved reminded me what we’ve been missing.

The imposing Elites are still the probably cleverest foes I’ve ever played against, and it’s been 25 years. They bark orders and duck away from my fire, and they know how to flank me, when to rush me and how to adapt to my assaults. Every time you die in this game, you come back to a slightly remixed firefight, making it endlessly replayable; I never minded going back to a checkpoint, because it never feels repetitious. In other shooters you simply memorise enemy numbers and positioning, but here you must constantly adapt your play, especially on higher Heroic or Legendary difficulty. And I’d somehow forgotten about the Hunters. The first time a pair of those spiked brutes appeared I reacted on pure decades-old muscle memory: I turned around and fled.

Unfortunately, we still must contend with the Flood. After several levels of brilliant open-ended fights against intelligent foes under the strange light of a foreign sun, suddenly we are transported into a boring, claustrophobic zombie shooter. I maintain that these mid-game levels are extremely bad: shooting 400 identical parasitic baddies with a shotgun while waiting for a floating robot to open a door has never been my idea of a good time. This will be a controversial opinion, but I was grateful for the new waypoints that told me exactly where to go in the maze of zombie-filled corridors that is the Library. It meant that the worst parts of this game were over sooner.

In co-op Halo becomes somewhat less challenging, atmospheric and tactical and significantly more chaotic. Especially when vehicles are involved, the game transforms completely with the addition of other players, thanks to its flexible, open level design and adaptable foes. I played through much of the game in split-screen with my partner – I maintain that playing Combat Evolved with four players just feels somehow wrong – and was reminded exactly why I spent hundreds of hours rinsing this game with friends as a teenager. Halo remains the best companionable shooting game out there.

Campaign Evolved is a good remake of a brilliant game. There are things that are worse: I miss the original Warthog’s erratic handling and the early-00s sci-fi aesthetic, which is simply irreproducible with modern graphics. For all its prettiness, this remake chugs along at times – especially in split-screen it would occasionally slow to a crawl, and we never had to worry about linking various different online accounts and connecting to servers when we fancied a quick game of Halo in 2001. But the core of this game is impossible to mess up. For millions of younger players, Campaign Evolved is a perfect, modernised introduction to everything that was great about the 00s-style first-person shooter. For those of us who were there at the time, it’s a welcome return trip.

Halo: Campaign Evolved is out now

title: FTSE 100 hits record high despite AI sell-off
description:
Strong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocks 
London’s FTSE 100 stock index has touched a fresh high, driven by strong corporate results as investors moved money away from tech and semiconductor stocks amid the global tech stock sell-off.

fullText:
Strong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocks

London’s FTSE 100 stock index has touched a fresh high, driven by strong corporate results as investors moved money away from tech and semiconductor stocks amid the global tech stock sell-off.

The UK’s blue chip index rose as high as 10,951 points on Wednesday morning before falling back slightly, its best level since 27 February, the day before the US and Israel began attacks on Iran and sparked stock market volatility.

On a day of fresh losses for the tech-heavy Nasdaq index, the FTSE 100 closed up 0.3% at 10,908, marginally below its record closing value of 10,910 in February.

The FTSE 100 is heavily weighted towards the finance and energy sectors, meaning it has been largely shielded from the sell-off in tech stocks that has rattled other global markets, particularly in Asia and New York.

The Asia-focused bank Standard Chartered and the miner Rio Tinto both announced a rise in shareholder payouts on Wednesday.

The FTSE 100’s climb came as shares in companies linked to AI plunged for the second day in a row over concerns about spending on the technology, sending stock markets in South Korea and Japan tumbling.

The oil price continued to climb after the US military said it had knocked down an Iranian missile barrage and worked with Saudi Arabia’s forces to strike sites in Iraq that Tehran-backed militias had recently used to launch attacks.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose above $90 a barrel by late afternoon in London, a rise of more than 7%.

Seoul’s Kospi index is dominated by semiconductor manufacturers, and disappointing results from the chipmaker SK Hynix left it down by as much as 12.6% at one point before it rebounded.

The index closed down 6% after falling almost 11% the previous day, reaching its lowest level since early April and marking an almost 40% fall from the peak reached a little over a month ago.

Trading was halted for 20 minutes for the second consecutive session after an 8% plunge triggered a market-wide circuit breaker.

Japan’s Nikkei also closed 1.5% down on Wednesday, a two-month low.

SK Hynix, which produces the chips essential to the expansion of AI datacentres, reported record profits for the second quarter but undershot investors’ expectations.

That prompted a sell-off that drove its shares down by as much as 20% before they recovered to 10% down. Shares in its fellow chipmaker Samsung Electronics also tumbled further, closing 5% lower.

The two companies together account for more than half of the market capitalisation of the Kospi, which has led to them holding sway over the market this year. The companies have brought in cash from investors looking to become involved in the lucrative AI trade amid a global shortage of advanced memory chips.

Analysts said disappointment over SK Hynix’s earnings highlighted investors’ concerns about how long tech companies could continue their spending spree on the technology.

“SK Hynix delivered strong results, but in today’s AI market strong is ‌no longer enough,” said Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore.

“Investors were looking for additional catalysts, particularly around long-term agreements and shareholder returns, to support a memory sector that has become the epicentre of the AI trade.”

Shares in US chip companies fell on Wall Street on Tuesday. Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology were all down.

Apple benefited from the falls as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven. Its shares briefly rose above the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark, only the second company ever to do so.

Shares in Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, fell 3% on Wednesday in Taipei.

Analysts said small-time investors had led the charge on buying chipmakers’ stocks, many using borrowed money. While this pushed stocks higher in last month’s rally, it has worsened the sell-off as many have pulled their money out.

South Korea’s finance minister, Koo Yun-cheol, told the national assembly the government was reviewing market stabilisation measures.

The broker AJ Bell’s investment director, Russ Mould, said the FTSE 100 had been “helped by its lack of exposure to technology and AI stocks, and a slew of strong corporate results, with index heavyweights Standard Chartered, Reckitt Benckiser and Rio Tinto all delivering either better-than-expected profits, or bumper cash returns to shareholders, or both”.

July 28 (Reuters) - U.S. stocks rebounded from earlier lows on Tuesday ahead of key corporate earnings releases and the Federal Reserve's highly anticipated interest rate decision on Wednesday.

World stocks had earlier fallen to a one-month low as ‌investors dumped chipmakers on concerns about Chinese competition and the funding of the AI boom.

But gains in other sectors offset a decline ‌in chip stocks in the U.S. session.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1.29% to 52,881.21, the S&P 500 rose 0.37% to 7,440.40 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.04% to 24,940.99.

Asian chipmakers ​were at the heart of Tuesday's earlier selloff, with South Korea's KOSPI diving more than 10% to a three-month low, triggering a circuit breaker on the way down as it heads for its largest monthly fall on record, surpassing declines suffered during the Asian financial crisis in 1997.

The index more than tripled in value over the 12 months to June, but has since shed more than a third of its value from that peak.

The MSCI All Country World Price index fell ‌0.26% to 1105, after earlier dropping to 1098, ⁠its lowest since June 26.

After a stellar rally this year, AI-linked stocks have been met with several bouts of selling in recent weeks as investors worry about stretched valuations and circular funding in the sector.

The latest rout followed a report ⁠that China had begun manufacturing domestically developed immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines, while Chinese chipmaker CXMT's strong stock-market debut on Monday fuelled concerns about increased competition in the memory chip industry.

There are concerns about the cost and the degree of leverage that needs to be taken on, said Dorian Carrell, head of multi-asset income at Schroders. "Now ​we're seeing ​questions over the profitability of the semiconductor space, particularly in Asia," he added.

Earnings this ​week from "Magnificent Seven" members Microsoft, Amazon.com, Meta and Apple, also ‌among companies that splurge the most on AI, will be seen as a key test of the market rally, particularly after Alphabet and Tesla spooked investors last week with negative cash flow reports.

OIL SLIDES, U.S. RATE MOVE EYED

A continued drop in oil prices and Treasury yields helped ease some nerves ahead of the Fed's rate decision that will come at the conclusion of its two-day meeting on Wednesday.

A surge in oil prices last week, driven by renewed fighting in the U.S.-Iran conflict, had raised expectations of a possible rate hike as policymakers grapple with inflation that remains stubbornly above the Fed's 2% ‌annual target.

title: AI Can Ride My Bike with No Handlebars
description: A 2008 alt-hip-hop hit holds the perfect warning for the artificial intelligence arms race and how big tech is weaponizing sci-fi hypotheticals to distract us from their own unchecked corporate power.
fullText:
I don’t remember the first time I heard Flobot’s Handlebars, but I have been hearing it a lot again recently in an attempt to connect with my past.

The song’s lyrics start with someone expressing happiness at the fact that they can ride a bicycle with no handlebars, and by the end, they threaten to end the world in a holocaust. There can be several interpretations of what any lyrics mean, but in this case, we can find a quote from the artist that clarifies the intended meaning:

The song is about the idea that we have so much incredible potential as human beings to be destructive or to be creative. And it’s tragic to me that the appetite for military innovation is endless, but when it comes to taking on a project like ending world hunger, it’s seen as outlandish. It’s not treated with the same seriousness… We have these little moments of creativity, these bursts of innovation, and every time that happens, that innovation is used to oppress and destroy people.

The song speaks about how scale almost always corrupts human innovation; that the same core innovation spirit in us that lets us find meaning and joy in simple acts like riding a bicycle with no handlebars can bring us meaning (and in some cases, joy) of guiding a missile with no satellite; that the human ego at scale is a dangerous thing.

Which brings us to the world of AI. Scale is everything in the world of artificial intelligence today, and it has been a big data center contest lately. The companies behind the frontier models have also scaled to extreme massive levels, with valuations hovering around hundreds of billions of dollars.

Perhaps the song is quite fitting for this narrative as well.

AI CEOs love talking about the end of the world for some reason. Another unqualified thing they often talk about is consciousness, with many frontier labs hinting that consciousness is just another milestone on the AI development roadmap, i.e., not only could their models represent and mimic people but actually be people. Almost all of them do not ponder much the ethical and moral implications of a truly conscious being in this context.

I think AI will probably, like, most likely sort of lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there will be great companies created with serious machine learning.

The idea that intelligent machines will destroy the world is not new. Many sci-fi works explore the situation; most involve a hyper-intelligent system that is either fully conscious as a being or can act as if it is. Most of them will not explain how it works, in the sense of how these computers or software turned into this thing.

The thing just shows up buck naked in a bar with a German accent and demands your clothes. It doesn’t tell you, “Oh yes, I understand what you’re saying and why you shall be curious. Yes, please sit down while I give you a presentation going through everything, all the scientific progress we made, how the machines actually work, what is consciousness and how we manipulate it, and et cetera.” That would make for a very boring movie.

Once we build a generally intelligent system, that basically we will ask it to figure out a way to make an investment return for you.

Consciousness is a subject that always seems to be at the center of the AI discussion but is never discussed seriously. For example, a tech CEO might boldly proclaim that their company will reach AGI (in fact, a specific form of conscious AGI) in the next three years. However, instead of following through on the legal, ethical, and philosophical framework of the company owning conscious beings, they would move on to how their ad business did 5% more year-over-year.

But is consciousness required or a part of the definition of AGI? The consensus seems to say no.

In recent times, we’ve also seen some pullback in the rhetoric, with leaders trying to define AGI as a capacity threshold rather than a claim of consciousness. For example, last year Sam Altman said: “I think it’s not a super useful term” when talking about AGI. It would be fair to assume that, instead of creating a living, breathing digital dog (which presumably is not just a matter of compute), the focus is now on creating a system that can replace human labor effectively, at least.

While a non-conscious AI system that can perform human tasks at a superlative capacity will mean you don’t need to worry about ethical and moral issues of deploying the said AI, it would still be a dangerous thing for society at large, just not in a Skynet type of way.

In his essay “The Adolescence of Technology”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proclaims seriously, “humanity is about to be handed almost unimaginable power, and it is deeply unclear whether we possess the maturity to wield it.” Most of the essay seems to be an argument for more regulations on AI; you can read it at your own risk and make up your mind on it.

Either way, skynet or no skynet, we can assume that if the AI arms race goes well, then in the worst case (from the point of view of AI companies) is that LLMs do not gain consciousness with more compute, but with better harnesses and integration, AI can become genuinely useful in every field to the point where the “controllers” of AI, i.e. the companies that control them, will be given an almost unimaginable power and it is deeply unclear if they have the maturity to wield it.

At that point, the worries expressed by Mr. Amodei in his essay become realistic concerns for everyone. However, if his answer can be found in the blog post that starts with “There is a scene in the movie version of Carl Sagan’s book Contact where the main character, an astronomer…”, I deem it not serious enough. By framing his essay with a romanticized sci-fi reference to the movie Contact, Amodei treats an immediate geopolitical and economic crisis as a philosophical thought experiment, skipping over the difficult questions of accountability. (I know that sounds rich coming from the person whose entire hook of the article is an late 2000s rap song, but still.)

Even on a rudimentary reading, he skips most of the difficult questions and focuses on things like billionaire philanthropy and preventing hardware access to oh-so-evil China. It is a great answer if you’re a billionaire and control the said AI, but it would be possible to argue that it is not the best answer, or the most ethical answer, or the fairest answer for all.

This brings me back to the song, and these particular lines:

I can hand out a million vaccinations / Or let ‘em all die in exasperation / Have ‘em all healed from their lacerations / Or have ‘em all killed by assassination / I can make anybody go to prison / Just because I don’t like ‘em / And I can do anything with no permission

A world where that stands true for private US companies like Google, OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic, or any private company does not sound like a good world. And it might be the world we are heading towards, AGI or no AGI.

It is a bit funny how tech CEOs will often claim that artificial intelligence, “the AI”, will take away x percent of jobs in y years. But they never say that their company will do it; they never say they’re investing billions hoping this happens, but rather “the AI” will take away the jobs and replace human beings, and we must be forewarned about such an evil winter that is to fall upon us.

Yet, from what we can see, there is no difference between OpenAI and the models it runs behind its closed doors, and the same for every private frontier AI lab. Yet there seems to be a sense that it’s acceptable to attribute full agency to the AI when it’s convenient while you own the shares and all financial gains.

You blame the same demon you command and profit from.

The moral problem in AI in this case isn’t really whether AI can be conscious or how to live in a world where that is true. But rather, should we trust in AI labs to be worthy of wielding such power? History tells us that no private entity is worthy of that power.

title: Nathaniel Hackett's "definitely a rookie" remark about Jeremiyah Love is getting overblown
description: We're in the business of finding and sharing and analyzing interesting remarks from anyone in the NFL ecosystem.
fullText:
We're in the business of finding and sharing and analyzing interesting remarks from anyone in the NFL ecosystem. But certain supposedly controversial comments aren't really as big of a deal as some may interpret them to be.

Case in point: Cardinals offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett is catching some heat for comments he made on Saturday about rookie running back Jeremiyah Love.

"He's definitely a rookie, and — as we've talked about," Hackett said. "And he'll keep growing every single day. I'm very excited for him. All those guys. Not just him."

The broader context has to be considered, especially since Hackett specifically added "as we've talked about."

Earlier in the session, Hackett addressed the challenges that first-year players face when training camp opens. The question related to the things that are different for rookies.

"Everything you can imagine," Hackett said. "I mean, coming to this league is — I mean, just the speed is so different. You talk about the speed, being in a new building. . . . [I]t's a whole new environment. New people to work with, and definitely new playbooks that are very, very intricate. Due to the fact of all the things that we see and all the different — I mean, just our defense out there. I mean, you get almost everything and more. Which is great, because it helps you for the season, but for a young player to have to be able to adjust and learn just basic system and then apply it to different defenses. It takes some time. So heads are spinning right now, especially after two days, but I think it'll just get better and better. That's the goal."

Hackett wasn't dismissing or minimizing Love. He's a rookie. Like the rest of the rookies. Everything is different. Everything is new. "Heads are spinning," as Hackett said.

Training camp is the time to slow, and eventually to stop, the spinning. They have plenty of time to get Love ready to go. For now, after only two days, he's beginning the adjustment.

That's all it means. Which makes the comment not nearly as alarming as some are making it out to be.

title: Years after basic income, participants share how their finances have changed
description: Business Insider talked to basic income participants years apart. They shared how their lives and finances changed after receiving cash payments.
fullText:
Hundreds of US cities tried cash payments for low-income households.

Business Insider reinterviewed participants years apart to see if their lives and finances changed.

They landed new jobs and bigger apartments, but still struggled to build long-term savings.

Cepia Harper arrived for her shift selling sneakers at an Atlanta Nike store around dinner time.

The 43-year-old spent the day teaching middle school English classes, grading papers, and checking in on her own three children. By the time she got to the store, she was ready to curl up on the couch, but she needed the part-time Nike gig to make ends meet for the month.

It's a contrast from where she was just two years ago. When reporters first spoke with Harper in spring 2024, she had just received her last $850 monthly check from a local basic income program and started a full-time teaching role. This summer, she's back to working multiple jobs as a single parent, but feels much more confident about the future.

Harper is one of thousands of Americans who have participated in guaranteed basic income programs. The model — heralded by advocates as a solution to poverty and housing insecurity in big cities — offers no-strings-attached cash to low-income households, typically for one to three years.

Business Insider has spoken with dozens of participants and pilot leaders across the country. Most recipients put the money toward rent, groceries, childcare, and emergency expenses. A handful spend the funds on higher education or job training to further their careers.

Tech leaders like Sam Altman and Elon Musk — alongside several left-leaning lawmakers — have previously advocated basic income pilots, especially in a job market increasingly reshaped by AI. But it it can be difficult to maintain the political will and budget to run the programs sustainably, and participants have shared mixed results about their long-term impact.

Participant data for these pilots is collected before, during, and immediately after receiving payments. What's less documented is how households fare in the years after their deposits stop. The jury's out on whether short-term financial support translates to long-term stability.

"That money helped me get my daughter to college, it helped me keep my kids out of trouble," Harper said. "It's not just a handout. It can change a person's life."

Do you have a story to share about guaranteed basic income or cost of living? Reach out to this reporter at allisonkelly@businessinsider.com.

Taniquewa Brewster, 41, has a new baby. The little girl she adopted babbles as she does chores around the apartment, or takes calls for work as an assistant property manager.

Brewster first spoke with Business Insider in fall 2024, soon after receiving $12,000 over one year from a GBI program in Austin. At the time, the mother of five was working overtime and barely covering essentials, which she said was "keeping me away from my family."

Part of the draw with basic income is the element of choice. Other social safety nets, like SNAP or Medicaid, are restricted to specific purposes, with households only able to spend the money on groceries or healthcare. With cash, advocates say that participants have more agency. They can cover a car repair, buy school supplies for their kids, or pay down debt.

Several basic income participants told Business Insider that being able to use the extra cash for childcare and education allowed them to forgo unstable, part-time jobs in favor of a more lucrative full-time job. Others said the money helped them afford a security deposit for an apartment, or pay for their child to participate in a sport. For some, it eased the burden of medical bills.

The vast majority of participants reported that cash increased their food and housing security, as well as their mental health and parent-child time, according to research from 27 US pilots across published by the nonprofit Mayors for a Guaranteed Income at the end of last year.

In June, Brewster said she earned the certifications she needed for a promotion with the help of basic income. She's on her way to "breaking the curse of generational poverty" for her children, she said, and feels stable about her housing situation for the first time in a while.

"It felt like people were actually asking me what my needs were, and how they could help me meet those needs," Brewster added. "There's something comforting about someone actually caring enough to ask."

It's been five years since Crystal Crawford lost her job as a social worker, and she's getting back on her feet. She said she participated in Georgia basic income program, which gave her $500 a month between December 2021 and 2022. The money helped her cover bills and boost her professional certifications. The 40-year-old has a new job as a community engagement specialist, and a business strategy side hustle.

"Having the flexibility to be able to pay for things — like being able to get your hair done for a potential interview — guaranteed income allowed me to do things that I probably would not have been able to do during that time," she said, adding that "financial hardship can happen to anyone."

Basic income hasn't been a magic fix for Crawford's financial concerns. She said she has student loan debt in deferment and hopes to start making payments soon. And the balance of her savings account is "definitely not where I want it to be."

Other former participants shared a similar sentiment with Business Insider. Some felt cash payments helped with short-term bills and professional development, but most pilots didn't run long enough to impact their longer-term finances. Many said their savings accounts and retirement outlook didn't materially improve. A few, but not all, said their annual earnings rose because of their career growth.

There are also hurdles to running a basic income program in the first place — let alone one that lasts longer than a few years. Some tech leaders who previously championed GBI for displaced workers have walked back their stance, saying that the payoff doesn't justify the investment. Critics of basic income also worry that no-string-attached cash could discourage participants from working, or that the taxpayer cost is too high alongside other safety net programs like Medicaid and SNAP.

The cost of running these programs typically falls on local governments and philanthropists, and cities often aren't able to maintain lasting political will to keep GBI funded, with some lawmakers worried they aren't broadly effective.

Harper plans to keep working part-time on top of her full-time teaching job for her own peace of mind. Years after her cash payments ended, she said one income simply isn't enough to raise a family.

Still, she credits GBI for helping her recover from one of the toughest times in her life.

"Before basic income, I was pretty much homeless," Harper said. "I was able to get a new apartment, substitute teach, and pay my rent because I had that extra income. Later, it led me to get a bigger apartment, and land an even better job."

fullText:
Reports of wide-scale replacement of workers by AI are overblown. Small businesses use it to help workers

I recently met the owner of a company that sells windows and doors. He told me he invested about $10,000 in an AI application that is used by his salespeople in his showroom. The application listens to the conversations between the salesperson and the prospective customer and then automatically creates a quote for the salesperson to review and send.

“It allows my salespeople to talk to more customers and spend less time doing paperwork,” he said. “And it cuts down on errors.”

Another businessperson I know connected Claude to a folder containing the specifications, manuals, instruction guides, technical sheets and other documentation for the equipment her company sells. She says that her customer-support team can now ask Claude questions on any issue and get quick answers. Her next step is to roll out the platform to her customers.

There are many more projects like these under way. Last year, most small businesses were using AI to get answers to questions, review contracts, create policies and rewrite emails. Now they’re starting to move into real-life applications that are showing true return on investment.

The AI story on Main Street seems so far to not be mass layoffs. It is exhausted owners using technology to help scarce employees do more work, make fewer mistakes and serve more customers.

Since mid-2021, the Department of Labor has reported an overall 9% increase – not decrease – of people employed. If you don’t believe the government, then read the numbers from HR and payroll processors such as ADP, Gusto and Paychex, who all report continued job gains among their customers – especially their smaller customers – during the same period of time. Gusto says that small businesses are expected to hire about 974,000 recent grads ages 20 to 24 in the 2026 season, up from 962,000 in 2025. There are almost 7.6m job openings this month, an increase from pre-Covid levels and most predominantly at small businesses. And recent surveys from numerous outlets have found that most small businesses – who employ half of the country’s workers – are not only optimistic about their growth but plan to hire more people in the coming months.

AI is not replacing people. And, despite media reports and the warnings from pundits, academics and experts, it’s not going to, at least for small companies. Why?

For starters, there just aren’t enough people to do the work that needs to be done. The US workforce is expected to significantly decline over the next decade, thanks to an ageing population and a slowdown in birthrates. Immigrant workers who perform much of our services are in short supply. Robot technology – even if a smaller company could afford them – is years away from installing dishwashers, fixing HVAC systems, laying pipes and putting up drywall. The construction industry is desperate for workers. Business owners now view AI as something that can help their workers do their jobs better while they’re easing into retirement.

People also adapt. It’s insulting when those experts say that millions will be unemployed, as if humans will just retreat into their darkened living rooms, collect some form of universal income check and watch Netflix all day. Humans aren’t like that.

When the tax code was first released in 1913, there were only a few dozen pages. Today it’s grown to tens of thousands. Twenty years ago, jobs like “social media manager”, “mobile app developer”, “executive coach”, “SEO specialist” and even “cannabis compliance manager” didn’t even exist. With all the automation and technology around us, how many times do you hear that someone is “slammed” or “hasn’t taken a vacation in years”? People want purpose and want to feel needed. They want to be busy. I believe humans will find plenty of other productive things to do with our time. Maybe the recent surge in entrepreneurship is indicative of that.

Also, it’s going to take a while to trust AI. My clients don’t. They don’t believe big tech’s promises that their data is protected and private when we regularly read of breaches and models trained on private information. They wonder if, by using AI platforms, their pricing, costs and other propriety information are being exposed for others to see. They’ve been burned by bugs, errors, shutdowns and disruptions before caused by unreliable technology, and they’re not stupid when today’s big tech companies cover up their tracks by saying these are just “hallucinations”. Please. There’s a long way to go before business owners in particular are going to let some bot process their invoices, collect receivables, interact with irate customers or be responsible for shipping products without human oversight.

Finally, big companies can lay off thousands of people without flinching because every big company has bloat. These jobs are generally in PR, marketing, IT and customer service and have always been exposed. Big companies often have entire departments where automation can quickly reduce headcount. Small businesses usually don’t. In a 20-person company, there is rarely much slack. Everyone’s valuable and needs to pull their weight. Like the windows-and-doors guy, they want AI to help their staff to do more in a day so they can stop just surviving and start growing.

Yes, technology throughout the years has replaced workers and the AI boom will do the same. Corporate America may use AI to cut jobs. Main Street is more likely to use it to save time, save margins and save the employees it already struggled to find. That is the AI story we should be paying more attention to.

fullText:
Artificial intelligence may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay

In March, Anthropic, the cutting-edge artificial intelligence business that gave us the chatbot Claude, published an analysis on the impact of AI on employment, to help us assess the claim that intelligent robots were about to redefine human existence, ending demand for human labor.

Last year in May, Anthropic’s co-founder, Dario Amodei, claimed AI could wipe out half of all entry-level jobs in one to five years. Last January, he told us AI would probably become a “general labor substitute for humans”. In June he said we risk “a world where the economic trade-off dial is stuck on the hypergrowth, hyper-inequality setting”.

And yet, Anthropic’s report suggests that, so far, AI’s impact has fallen short of expectations: “We find no systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022,” the report stated. Deployment of the technology “remains a fraction of what’s feasible”. Claude covers just 33% of all tasks in the computer and math category whereas theoretically it could take over nearly 100% of them.

Spending on datacenters is going through the roof, for sure, but productivity has not been experiencing the galloping gains that the technorati’s epochal prognostications lead one to expect. Labor productivity was, in fact, slower in the first three years of our AI era than during the information technology boom that began in the mid 1990s.

Even OpenAI’s Sam Altman, AI’s most public face, says he now doubts its job-killing potential. “I don’t think we’re going to have the kind ​of jobs apocalypse that some of the companies in our space advocate or talk about,” he said in May. As Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist David Autor noted: “A lot of people have noticed that the world is not changing as fast as they predicted.”

This has opened the public conversation to a less cataclysmic narrative of the evolution of the technology. The emerging new story not only puts more emphasis on the complexity of the relationship between automation and human work across history. It is also raising doubts about the very feasibility of the threatened AI transformation of the universe. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index, which had been propelled almost exclusively by the rise of AI-related stocks, has fallen about 8% since its peak in early June.

One strand of critique of the “AI-will-do-everything” story might be called the O-ring argument. It comes from the mid-flight explosion of the space shuttle Challenger 73 seconds into its flight on 28 January 1986. A lengthy investigation concluded that the demise of the multibillion dollar spaceship was caused by a rubber O-ring that didn’t work at low temperatures.

That cheap O-ring proved critical. The analogy suggests that as long as AI cannot perform every task perfectly, it will increase the value of the remaining tasks. Depending on which the AI takes over, it could increase the value of high skill workers who are relieved by AI of the low-end part of their job, or increase the opportunity of lower skilled workers by taking over the more expert tasks.

As one recent study noted: “despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.”

Things could change. As Jed Kolko points out, research on the labor market impact of artificial intelligence is still in its infancy. There are almost four years to go in Amodei’s one-to-five year window. And maybe devastation hits in year six. According to the Federal Reserve, adoption of AI is expanding fast across businesses.

Moreover, Autor argues, AI is getting better. And its progress shows no sign that it will soon hit a ceiling. “Skepticism about the stochastic parrot is behind us,” he told me. The dystopian AI future – utopian, if you get to own and run the AI – is still on the cards.

“Insiders are as gung ho as ever,” noted Daron Acemoglu, the Nobel prize-winning economist. “They still believe artificial general intelligence is around the corner.” Indeed, Elon Musk has not budged from the dream that “AI+Robots will be able to do everything, resulting in universal high income. Work will be optional.”

One may recall the quip by Nobel prize-winning economist Robert Solow in the early years of the computer revolution: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” It took another 10 years or so, as businesses reorganized around the new technology. But computers did eventually show up in the stats.

Clouds are nonetheless gathering on the AI horizon. It’s not just that AI may not end all human work. AI may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay.

The politics have decidedly soured on the project. Seven in 10 Americans oppose building AI datacenters in their area. While this has to do with their insatiable demand for energy, which drives up local electricity costs, AI’s unpopularity is no doubt related to the proposition that it will destroy society as we know it.

There are other bumps in the road. Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs. “Not everything is a computational problem,” notes Autor. AI is good at replicating language, but it cannot connect language to the reality around it. Despite its progress, it still makes plenty of critical mistakes.

And then there are the impossible economics. Even if AI could eventually solve all our problems, the solution looks expensive. How much of GDP are we willing to invest in AI datacenters, 20%? 30%? 40%? According to some estimates, that is where we are headed. The International Energy Agency estimates that power demand from datacenters will more than double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, more than the energy consumption of Japan.

The economics look more fragile considering how fast the investment in AI depreciates, as new models overtake those developed just a few months ago. Companies developing AI models “are never going to make money”, Acemoglu said. “They are losing hundreds of billions of dollars every year.”

One may discount Altman’s new modesty as a PR feint. Somebody may have told him that equating the AI revolution with mass joblessness was not smart politics. But misgivings about AI’s vaunted capabilities are more than a marketing twist. The grand, epochal promise may be in trouble. Maybe artificial intelligence can’t deliver at a price society is willing to pay.
